claim: Huntington's disease is characterized by the formation of neuronal intracellular inclusions and loss of striatal projection neurons.
source: Huntington's disease (HD), an inherited neurodegenerative disorder, is characterized by the formation of neuronal intracellular inclusions and loss of striatal projection neurons (Reiner et al., 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reiner et al., 1988.

claim: The underlying cause of Huntington's disease is due to an abnormal expansion of the CAG tract beyond 35–40 repeats in Exon 1 of the Huntingtin gene.
source: The underlying cause of this disease is due to an abnormal expansion of the CAG (coding for the amino acid, Glutamine, Q) tract beyond 35–40 repeats in Exon 1 of the Huntingtin gene (MacDonald, 1993), which may promote an abnormal protein conformation, resulting in the formation of aggregates observed in the nucleus and cytoplasm of affected neurons (Lunkes et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to MacDonald, 1993 and Lunkes et al., 1999.

claim: Huntingtin aggregates are capable of spreading from cell to cell in the Drosophila brain, resulting in a loss of the neuronal population.
source: Huntingtin aggregates are capable of spreading from cell – to – cell in the Drosophila brain, resulting in a loss of the neuronal population. However, neuronal loss could be prevented by blocking endocytosis in the recipient neurons or synaptic exocytosis (Babcock and Ganetzky, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Babcock and Ganetzky, 2015.

claim: Neuronal loss caused by Huntingtin aggregates could be prevented by blocking endocytosis in the recipient neurons or synaptic exocytosis.
source: However, neuronal loss could be prevented by blocking endocytosis in the recipient neurons or synaptic exocytosis (Babcock and Ganetzky, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Babcock and Ganetzky, 2015.

claim: Mutant forms of Huntingtin affect non-neuronal cells in addition to neurons.
source: In addition to affecting neurons, mutant forms of Huntingtin also affect other non-neuronal cells (Sathasivam et al., 1999; Weiss et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sathasivam et al., 1999 and Weiss et al., 2012.

claim: Abnormalities in the peripheral, non-CNS tissues of HD patients are consistently observed, resulting in weight loss, altered glucose homeostasis, and sub-cellular abnormalities.
source: Abnormalities in the peripheral, non-CNS tissues of HD patients are consistently observed, resulting in weight loss, altered glucose homeostasis, and sub-cellular abnormalities (Sassone et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sassone et al., 2009.

claim: Aberrant immune responses are observed in the presence of Huntingtin aggregates.
source: Aberrant immune responses are observed in the presence of Huntingtin aggregates (Nayak et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nayak et al., 2011.

claim: Expression of Huntingtin aggregates resulted in a compromised immune function in Drosophila hemocytes resulting in increased susceptibility to infections, and altered production of cytokines and JAK-Stat pathway activity.
source: Expression of Huntingtin aggregates resulted in a compromised immune function in Drosophila hemocytes resulting in increased susceptibility to infections, and altered production of cytokines and JAK-Stat pathway activity (Lin et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lin et al., 2019.

claim: An effective immune response is largely dependent on functional endocytosis.
source: An effective immune response is largely dependent on functional endocytosis (Devergne et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Devergne et al., 2007 and Huang et al., 2010.

claim: Internalization of transferrin was drastically reduced in the presence of aggregated forms of Huntingtin and other pathogenic polyQ aggregates, suggestive of altered endocytosis.
source: Interestingly, internalization of transferrin, a cargo internalized via clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) was drastically reduced in the presence of aggregated forms of Huntingtin and other pathogenic polyQ aggregates, suggestive of altered endocytosis (Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2014.

claim: CME plays a critical role in synaptic vesicle trafficking.
source: CME plays a critical role in synaptic vesicle trafficking (Royle and Lagnado, 2010), with clathrin-coated structures (CCSs) being central to this process (Conner and Schmid, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Royle and Lagnado, 2010.

claim: Clathrin-coated structures (CCSs) are central to the process of synaptic vesicle trafficking.
source: CME plays a critical role in synaptic vesicle trafficking (Royle and Lagnado, 2010), with clathrin-coated structures (CCSs) being central to this process (Conner and Schmid, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Conner and Schmid, 2003.

claim: Alterations in CME have been implicated in neurodegenerative disorders such as Huntington's disease, spinocerebellar ataxia type I and Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
source: Alterations in CME have also been implicated in neurodegenerative disorders such as Huntington's disease, spinocerebellar ataxia type I and Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text without specific citation in this sentence, but is supported by the broader context of the manuscript.

claim: Protein aggregates formed by mutant forms of Huntingtin (HTT), Ataxin-1 (Atx1) and Superoxide dismutase-1 (SOD1) can inhibit CME and AMPA receptor recycling.
source: Previous reports demonstrate that protein aggregates formed by mutant forms of Huntingtin (HTT), Ataxin-1 (Atx1) and Superoxide dismutase-1 (SOD1) can inhibit CME and AMPA receptor recycling (Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2014.

claim: The polyQ containing Huntingtin exon 1 fragment interacts with proteins involved in CME including the Clathrin heavy chain, Huntingtin interacting protein 1 (Hip1), Adaptor protein complex 2 alpha 2 subunit and Dynamin1.
source: The polyQ containing Huntingtin exon 1 fragment is also known to interact with proteins involved in CME including the Clathrin heavy chain, Huntingtin interacting protein 1 (Hip1), Adaptor protein complex 2 alpha 2 subunit and Dynamin1 (Kaltenbach et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kaltenbach et al., 2007.

claim: Uptake of transferrin was reduced in the presence of Huntington aggregates.
source: Further, uptake of transferrin, a ligand that undergoes endocytosis was reduced in the presence of Huntington aggregates, while mutations in genes involved in endocytosis enhanced Huntington-associated toxicity (Meriin et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Meriin et al., 2003.

claim: Mutations in genes involved in endocytosis enhanced Huntington-associated toxicity.
source: Further, uptake of transferrin, a ligand that undergoes endocytosis was reduced in the presence of Huntington aggregates, while mutations in genes involved in endocytosis enhanced Huntington-associated toxicity (Meriin et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Meriin et al., 2003.

claim: Actin plays a central and critical role in the context of CME.
source: Actin is known to play a central and critical role in the context of CME (Merrifield et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Merrifield et al., 2002.

claim: Alterations in the organization of actin regulate the physical properties of cells.
source: Alterations in the organization of actin are known to regulate the physical properties of cells (Mote et al., 2020), which in turn are shown to impact the health and function of cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mote et al., 2020.

claim: Loss of Huntingtin resulted in hyperactivation of LIM kinase and stabilized the Actin cytoskeleton in a Cofilin-dependent manner.
source: A recent study, using Huntingtin knockout mice demonstrated that loss of Huntingtin resulted in hyperactivation of LIM kinase and stabilized the Actin cytoskeleton in a Cofilin-dependent manner (Wennagel et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wennagel et al., 2022.

claim: The movement and directionality of CCSs are affected in the presence of pathogenic Huntingtin aggregates.
source: Our study reveals that the movement and directionality of CCSs are affected in the presence of pathogenic Huntingtin aggregates, accompanied by alterations in actin flow in Drosophila hemocytes and mammalian cells.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding of the current study and is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pathogenic forms of Huntingtin disrupt actin reorganization by sequestering Arp2/3 complex components and actin.
source: We further demonstrate that pathogenic forms of Huntingtin disrupt actin reorganization by sequestering Arp2/3 complex components and actin, with overexpression of either Arp3 or Hip1 partially rescuing the stalled CCS movement phenotype along with restoring their directional movement.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding of the current study and is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Overexpression of either Arp3 or Hip1 partially rescues the stalled CCS movement phenotype and restores directional movement in cells with Huntingtin aggregates.
source: We further demonstrate that pathogenic forms of Huntingtin disrupt actin reorganization by sequestering Arp2/3 complex components and actin, with overexpression of either Arp3 or Hip1 partially rescuing the stalled CCS movement phenotype along with restoring their directional movement.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding of the current study and is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Arp3 or Hip1 overexpression rescued Huntingtin-driven neurodegeneration observed in the Drosophila eye.
source: Arp3 or Hip1 overexpression also rescued Huntingtin-driven neurodegeneration observed in the Drosophila eye.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding of the current study and is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cells containing Huntingtin aggregates display an increased cellular stiffness in an actin-dependent manner.
source: Using atomic force microscopy (AFM), we determined that cells containing Huntingtin aggregates display an increased cellular stiffness in an actin-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding of the current study using AFM and is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Overexpression of Hip1 or transient treatment with Latrunculin A restored cellular stiffness to levels comparable to wild type cells.
source: Interestingly, overexpression of Hip1 or transient treatment with Latrunculin A restored cellular stiffness to levels comparable to wild type cells.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding of the current study and is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TDP-43 displayed defective CME, altered actin organization and increased stiffness, similar to pathogenic Huntingtin.
source: Examination of other pathogenic aggregates revealed that TDP-43 also displayed defective CME, altered actin organization and increased stiffness, similar to pathogenic Huntingtin.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding of the current study and is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is an intimate connection between dysfunctional CME, actin misorganization and increased cellular stiffness caused by alteration in the local intracellular environment by pathogenic aggregates.
source: Together, our results point to an intimate connection between dysfunctional CME, actin misorganization and increased cellular stiffness caused by alteration in the local intracellular environment by pathogenic aggregates.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion of the current study based on the presented data.

claim: Aggregation and misfolding of proteins is often linked to a number of neurodegenerative disorders such as Huntington's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disorder.
source: Aggregation and misfolding of proteins is often linked to a number of neurodegenerative disorders such as Huntington's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disorder (DiFiglia et al., 1997; Chartier-Harlin et al., 1991; Bruijn et al., 1997; Davies et al., 1997; Wilson et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster expressing mutant forms of the Huntingtin gene display many of the phenotypes observed in affected human patients, including accumulation of protein aggregates in cells and reduced life span.
source: Previous reports have demonstrated that Drosophila melanogaster expressing mutant forms of the Huntingtin gene display many of the phenotypes observed in affected human patients, including accumulation of protein aggregates in cells and reduced life span (Weiss et al., 2012; Rosas-Arellano et al., 2018; Bradford et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Weiss et al., 2012; Rosas-Arellano et al., 2018; Bradford et al., 2010.

claim: Non-neuronal Drosophila cells display altered cellular properties in the presence of pathogenic Huntingtin aggregates.
source: Further, non-neuronal Drosophila cells also display altered cellular properties in the presence of pathogenic Huntingtin aggregates (Lin et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lin et al., 2019.

claim: Cells containing Huntingtin aggregates display reduced transferrin uptake indicating that endocytosis may be compromised.
source: Other reports have demonstrated that cells containing Huntingtin aggregates display reduced transferrin uptake indicating that endocytosis may be compromised (Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2014.

claim: In WT or non-pathogenic HTT Q15 expressing hemocytes, CCSs show centripetal movement.
source: In the WT or non-pathogenic HTT Q15 (data not shown) expressing hemocytes, we observed a centripetal movement of CCSs similar to previous observations (Kochubey et al., 2006; Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kochubey et al., 2006 and by data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: In HTT Q138 expressing cells there was little to no movement of CCSs.
source: However, in HTT Q138 expressing cells there was little to no movement of these CCSs (Figure 1B; Figure 1—video 1, Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and associated videos.

claim: In WT/HTT Q15 expressing cells, CCSs follow a specific path with defined speeds.
source: Using particle image velocimetry (PIV) analysis (see Materials and methods for details and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) to quantify the movement and directionality of CCSs, we determined that in WT/HTT Q15 expressing cells, CCSs follow a specific path with defined speeds (Figure 1A'), whereas CCSs in HTT Q138 expressing cells do not show any directional movement, with negligible radial speed indicating a severe compromise in clathrin dynamics and movement of clathrin-coated structures (Figure 1B').
evidence: The claim is supported by PIV analysis data shown in Figure 1A'.

claim: CCSs in HTT Q138 expressing cells do not show any directional movement, with negligible radial speed indicating a severe compromise in clathrin dynamics and movement of clathrin-coated structures.
source: Using particle image velocimetry (PIV) analysis (see Materials and methods for details and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) to quantify the movement and directionality of CCSs, we determined that in WT/HTT Q15 expressing cells, CCSs follow a specific path with defined speeds (Figure 1A'), whereas CCSs in HTT Q138 expressing cells do not show any directional movement, with negligible radial speed indicating a severe compromise in clathrin dynamics and movement of clathrin-coated structures (Figure 1B').
evidence: The claim is supported by PIV analysis data shown in Figure 1B'.

claim: HTT Q138 expressing hemocytes showed reduced colocalization of mBSA with CCSs coupled with reduced internalization in comparison to control hemocytes.
source: HTT Q138 expressing hemocytes showed reduced colocalization of mBSA with CCSs coupled with reduced internalization in comparison to control hemocytes (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: A loss in movement of CCSs was observed exclusively in the presence of HTT Q138 aggregates in mammalian cells HEK293T and SH-SY5Y, similar to what was observed in hemocytes.
source: We also determined the movement of CCSs in mammalian cells, HEK293T and SH-SY5Y expressing either HTT Q15 or HTT Q138. We observed a loss in movement of CCSs exclusively in the presence of HTT Q138 aggregates, similar to what was observed in hemocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating the existence of similar deficits across cell types and organisms.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The centripetal CCS movement in hemocytes was dependent on the actin cytoskeleton and not on microtubules.
source: Previously using inhibitors such as Latrunculin A, colchicine or nocodazole, it was shown that the centripetal CCS movement in hemocytes was dependent on the actin cytoskeleton and not on microtubules (Kochubey et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kochubey et al., 2006.

claim: The role of the actin cytoskeleton is well established in the context of CME and CCS movement across various mammalian cell lines and in yeast.
source: The role of the actin cytoskeleton is also well established in the context of CME and CCS movement across various mammalian cell lines and in yeast (Meriin et al., 2003; Yarar et al., 2005; Ferguson et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Meriin et al., 2003; Yarar et al., 2005; Ferguson et al., 2009.

claim: Hemocytes treated with Latrunculin A or Cytochalasin D showed severe retardation in CCS movement in comparison to their DMSO treated counterparts.
source: Similar to what was previously reported, we found that hemocytes treated with pharmacological inhibitors of actin polymerization, Latrunculin A (LatA) or Cytochalasin D (CytoD) showed severe retardation in CCS movement in comparison to their DMSO treated counterparts (Figure 2A and B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment with Latrunculin A or Cytochalasin D was accompanied by a loss of CCSs speed, directionality and centripetal movement.
source: This was also accompanied by a loss of CCSs speed, directionality and centripetal movement (Figure 2A', A'', B' and B'').
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A', A'', B' and B''.

claim: Actin-GFP was sequestered in HTT Q138 aggregates.
source: To further understand how HTT Q138 impacted actin function, we co-expressed Actin-GFP along with HTT Q138. We observed sequestration of Actin-GFP in the HTT aggregates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a dramatic alteration in the dynamics of actin and reduced filopodia number and length in HTT Q138 expressing cells.
source: While we observed a dynamic actin cytoskeleton accompanied by numerous filopodia extensions and retractions in WT/HTT Q15 expressing cells, there was a dramatic alteration in the dynamics of actin and reduced filopodia number and length in HTT Q138 expressing cells (Figure 2C, D and E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—video 1 and Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C, D and E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and associated videos.

claim: The thickness and intensity of cortical actin was significantly increased in presence of HTT Q138 compared to HTT Q15 expressing cells.
source: Measurement of cortical actin revealed that the thickness as well as intensity was significantly increased in presence of HTT Q138 compared to HTT Q15 expressing cells (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: A significant reduction of incorporated actin was observed in HTT Q138 expressing cells, indicating that polymerization of actin was hampered.
source: To study the polymerization of actin in HTT Q15/Q138 expressing cells, we performed barbed end labelling of actin by providing fluorescently tagged actin, similar to what has been previously described (Pardee and Spudich, 1982). A significant reduction of incorporated actin was observed in HTT Q138 expressing cells (Figure 2H I), indicating that polymerization of actin was hampered in the presence of HTT Q138.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2H and I, and by citation to Pardee and Spudich, 1982.

claim: There was a reduction in actin flow in hemocytes expressing HTT Q138 compared to WT cells.
source: This was further supported by a reduction in actin flow in hemocytes expressing HTT Q138 compared to WT cells (Figure 2J).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Formation of filopodia requires the activity of the Arp2/3 complex.
source: Formation of filopodia requires the activity of the Arp2/3 complex (Korobova and Svitkina, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Korobova and Svitkina, 2008.

claim: Mass spectrometric analysis of Huntingtin aggregates formed in the brain indicated a sequestration of a number of proteins involved in actin remodeling and endocytosis.
source: Mass spectrometric analysis of Huntingtin aggregates formed in the brain indicated a sequestration of a number of proteins involved in actin remodeling and endocytosis. Among these were components of the Arp2/3 complex, additional actin-modulating proteins, clathrin heavy and light chains and Hip1 and Hip1r, proteins that are known to connect clathrin pits to actin at sites of endocytosis, although the nature of their sequestration and association with aggregates remains unknown (Hosp et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hosp et al., 2017 and Kim et al., 2016.

claim: Significant enrichment of Arp3 was found within HTT Q138 aggregates.
source: Similar to what was previously demonstrated, we found significant enrichment of Arp3, a key component of the Arp2/3 complex within HTT Q138 aggregates (Figure 3A) indicating atleast a partial sequestration of one of the components of the Arp2/3 complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Inducing expression of a transgenic Arp3 RNAi construct in hemocytes resulted in a reduction in the number of filopodia along with stalled movement of CCSs and loss of directional movement.
source: Upon inducing expression of a transgenic Arp3 RNAi construct in hemocytes, we observed a reduction in the number of filopodia (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) along with stalled movement of CCSs (Figure 3C and C') and loss of directional movement (Figure 3C'').
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B, C, C', C'' and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment of wild type cells with CK666, a chemical inhibitor of Arp2/3, resulted in stalled CCS movement.
source: Similar results were also obtained upon treatment of wild type cells with CK666, a chemical inhibitor of Arp2/3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Knockdown of Profilin in hemocytes resulted in an impairment in CCS movement as well as actin dynamics.
source: Knockdown of Profilin in hemocytes also resulted in an impairment in CCS movement as well as actin dynamics (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Chemical inhibition of Formin by SMIFH2 resulted in stalled CCS movement.
source: Chemical inhibition of Formin, a Rho GTPase involved in regulation of elongation of actin fibers by SMIFH2, also resulted in stalled CCS movement (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), further establishing that remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton is required for directional movement of CCSs.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Recovery of fluorescence intensity of Clc-GFP was severely compromised in the presence of HTT Q138 compared to an almost complete recovery in wild type and control cells.
source: Recovery of fluorescence intensity of Clc-GFP was severely compromised in the presence of HTT Q138 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) compared to an almost complete recovery in wild type and control (Luc VAL 10) cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Incomplete recovery of Clc-GFP was observed upon knocking down Profilin or upon treatment with Lat A.
source: Incomplete recovery was also observed upon knocking down Profilin or upon treatment with Lat A (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The organization and dynamics of microtubules remained unchanged even in the presence of Huntingtin aggregates.
source: We found that the organization and dynamics of microtubules remained unchanged even in the presence of Huntingtin aggregates (Figure 3—videos 1 and 2) supporting the previous finding (Kochubey et al., 2006) that microtubules do not play a role in early events of CME.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—videos 1 and 2, and by citation to Kochubey et al., 2006.

claim: Huntingtin is known to interact with Myosin VI via its optineurin binding domain.
source: Huntingtin is known to interact with Myosin VI via its optineurin binding domain (Caviston and Holzbaur, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Caviston and Holzbaur, 2009.

claim: Myosin VI is implicated in various steps of membrane trafficking and shown to be involved in trafficking of clathrin-coated vesicles.
source: The actin-based cytoskeleton motor, Myosin VI, is also implicated in various steps of membrane trafficking Buss et al., 2001b and shown to be involved in trafficking of clathrin-coated vesicles (Soldati and Schliwa, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Buss et al., 2001b and Soldati and Schliwa, 2006.

claim: Myosin VI is associated with CCSs through its C-terminal tail.
source: It has also been shown that Myosin VI is associated with CCSs through its C –terminal tail Buss et al., 2001a.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Buss et al., 2001a.

claim: The coordinated action of myosin VI and Clathrin light chain a (CLCa) are essential for the fission of clathrin-coated pits.
source: The coordinated action of myosin VI and Clathrin light chain a (CLCa) are essential for the fission of clathrin-coated pits (Biancospino et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Biancospino et al., 2019.

claim: Knocking down Myosin VI resulted in an impairment of CCS movement.
source: Knocking down Myosin VI, resulted in an impairment of CCS movement (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—video 3.

claim: Knocking down Myosin VI had no discernible effect on actin dynamics or on filopodia formation.
source: However there was no discernible effect on actin dynamics or on filopodia formation (Figure 3—video 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—video 4.

claim: Co-expressing Arp3 along with pathogenic HTT Q138 in hemocytes resulted in a partial restoration of CCS movement and directionality along with filopodia formation.
source: Towards this we co-expressed Arp3 along with pathogenic HTT Q138 in hemocytes and used live cell imaging to check the status of CCS movement and actin dynamics in these cells. We observed a partial restoration of CCS movement and directionality along with filopodia formation (Figure 4A, A', A'' and 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—video 1 and Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A, A', A'', 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and associated videos.

claim: Hip1 is one of several proteins involved in the initial stages of Clathrin mediated endocytosis.
source: Huntingtin interacting protein1 (Hip1) is one of several proteins involved in the initial stages of Clathrin mediated endocytosis (Metzler et al., 2001; Engqvist-Goldstein et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Metzler et al., 2001 and Engqvist-Goldstein et al., 2001.

claim: Hip1 is a known interactor of Huntingtin protein and expansions in the polyglutamate tract disrupt this interaction.
source: Hip1 is also a known interactor of Huntingtin protein and expansions in the polyglutamate tract, as seen in pathological conditions, are known to disrupt this interaction (Kalchman et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kalchman et al., 1997.

claim: Hip1 is known to interact with actin and the Hip1-actin interaction is known to be regulated by the clathrin light chain.
source: Additionally, Hip1 is also known to interact with actin Senetar et al., 2004 and the Hip1-actin interaction is known to be regulated by the clathrin light chain (Wilbur et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Senetar et al., 2004 and Wilbur et al., 2008.

claim: Hip1 was found to be sequestered in pathogenic Huntingtin aggregates.
source: Further, as previously mentioned, Hip1 was also found to be sequestered in pathogenic Huntingtin aggregates (Hosp et al., 2017; Qin et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hosp et al., 2017 and Qin et al., 2004.

claim: Co-expressing Hip1 with pathogenic HTT Q138 resulted in a partial rescue of CCS movement.
source: Upon co-expressing Hip1 with pathogenic HTT Q138, we observed a partial rescue of CCS movement (Figure 4B, B' and B'', and Figure 4—video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B, B', B'' and Figure 4—video 3.

claim: Knocking down Hip1 in wild type hemocytes resulted in a reduction in movement, speed, and loss of directionality of CCSs.
source: Conversely, knocking down Hip1 in wild type hemocytes resulted in a reduction in movement (Figure 4C), speed, and loss of directionality of CCSs (Figure 4C' and C''), thus highlighting the importance of the Hip1- actin axis in CME and its possible disruption in the presence of HTT Q138.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C, C' and C''.

claim: Drosophila Mrj, a homologue of mammalian DnaJB6, was observed to rescue polyglutamine associated toxicity in Drosophila.
source: Previously, Drosophila Mrj, a homologue of mammalian DnaJB6 was observed to rescue polyglutamine associated toxicity in Drosophila.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text without a specific citation in this sentence, but is supported by the broader context.

claim: DNAJB6, a member of the DNAJ (HSP40) chaperone family, was found to efficiently suppress polyQ aggregation in cells.
source: In a screen for polyQ modifiers, DNAJB6, a member of the DNAJ (HSP40) chaperone family was found to efficiently suppress polyQ aggregation in cells (Hageman et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hageman et al., 2010.

claim: PolyQ toxicity and aggregation can be modulated by DNAJ chaperones in mice and Drosophila.
source: Previous studies in mice and Drosophila have also shown that polyglutamine toxicity and aggregation can be modulated by DNAJ chaperones (Labbadia et al., 2012; Warrick et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Labbadia et al., 2012 and Warrick et al., 1999.

claim: Mrj can effectively suppress polyQ toxicity.
source: The DNAJ domain containing protein Mrj, which is highly enriched in the brain, can effectively suppress polyQ toxicity (Chuang et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chuang et al., 2002.

claim: Mrj was identified in an independent screen to modulate the cytotoxicity in the context of protein aggregation.
source: Additionally, Mrj was also identified in an independent screen to modulate the cytotoxicity in the context of protein aggregation (Desai et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Desai et al., 2022.

claim: Coexpressing Mrj along with HTT Q138 in hemocytes partially restored CCS movement, speed and directionality along with filopodia formation.
source: We found that coexpressing Mrj along with HTT Q138 in hemocytes partially restored CCS movement (Figure 4D) speed and directionality (Figure 4D' and D'' and Figure 4—video 4) along with filopodia formation (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D, D', D'', 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—video 4.

claim: Overexpression of either Arp3, Hip1 or Mrj could rescue the neurodegeneration observed in Drosophila eyes caused by the overexpression of pathogenic HTT Q127.
source: Additionally, overexpression of either Arp3, Hip1 or Mrj could also rescue the neurodegeneration observed in Drosophila eyes caused by the overexpression of pathogenic HTT Q127 (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Cells expressing HTT Q138 were stiffer than WT cells, as indicated by the higher Young's modulus.
source: Our results demonstrated that cells expressing HTT Q138 were stiffer than WT cells, as indicated by the higher Young's modulus (or stiffness; Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The stiffness of cells expressing pathogenic Huntingtin aggregates was partially rescued upon overexpression of either Hip1 or Mrj.
source: The stiffness of cells expressing pathogenic Huntingtin aggregates was partially rescued upon overexpression of either Hip1 or Mrj (Figure 5A) indicating that partial restoration in actin organization may also rescue stiffness of these cells in addition to CME.
evidence: The claim is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Treatment of CK666 led to a decrease in stiffness of cells compared to DMSO-treated cells.
source: We performed AFM on cells treated with CK666, a inhibitor of the Arp2/3 complex and found that treatment of CK666 led to a decrease in stiffness of cells compared to DMSO-treated cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cells treated with LatA showed decreased stiffness in comparison to DMSO-treated cells.
source: We also noticed a decreased stiffness of cells upon LatA treatment in comparison to DMSO-treated cells (Figure 5A) suggesting that an altered state of the cytoskeleton was largely responsible for contributing to the increased stiffness observed in the presence of HTT Q138.
evidence: The claim is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A brief, transient treatment of Lat A to HTT Q138 cells resulted in movement of CCSs at an intermediate time point.
source: We were able to see movement of CCSs in these cells at an intermediate time point (Figure 5B) thereby strengthening the idea that CCS movement requires a dynamic form of the actin cytoskeleton and that HTT Q138 causes the cytoskeleton to be held in a very stiff state.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the presence of TDP-43, a significant reduction in CCS movement was observed, similar to what was observed in the presence of HTT Q138.
source: We observed that while Aβ–42–2 x, FUSR521C (FUS), αSynA30P or αSynA53T (Figure 6A and Figure 6—video 1–4) caused no defect in CCS movement, in the presence of TDP-43 we noticed a significant reduction in CCS movement (Figure 6A and B and Figure 6—video 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and B and Figure 6—video 5.

claim: CCSs moved inwards in all cases except TDP-43 expressing cells, in which movement was completely stalled.
source: Tracking and quantification of CCSs in WT cells and cells expressing mutant proteins revealed that CCSs moved inwards in all cases, except TDP-43 expressing cells, in which movement was completely stalled (Figure 6A and B and Figure 6—video 5), similar to what we observed in the presence of HTT Q138.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and B and Figure 6—video 5.

claim: The mean instantaneous velocities showed a significant decrease in the presence of TDP-43.
source: This was also supported by analysis of the mean instantaneous velocities, which showed a significant decrease in the presence of TDP-43 (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The uptake of fluorescently tagged mBSA was markedly reduced in the presence of TDP-43 indicative of a reduction in CME.
source: Additionally, the uptake of fluorescently tagged mBSA was markedly reduced in the presence of TDP-43 (Figure 6D) indicative of a reduction in CME.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Recovery of clathrin was severely compromised only in the presence of TDP-43, similar to HTT Q138.
source: Recovery of clathrin was severely compromised only in the presence of TDP-43, similar to HTT Q138, and was indistinguishable from WT in the context of other aggregates (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A dramatic reduction in filopodia formation was noticed in the presence of TDP-43.
source: Here again, we saw no significant difference in filopodia formation in the hemocytes expressing Aβ–42–2 x (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—video 1), FUSR521C (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—video 2) or both mutants of α-Synuclein (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—videos 3 and 4), but noticed a dramatic reduction in the presence of TDP–43 (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, and Figure 7—video 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, and Figure 7—video 5.

claim: Number, length and lifetime of filopodia were compromised in the presence of TDP-43 expressing cells as compared to wild type cells.
source: Number, length and lifetime of filopodia were also compromised in the presence of TDP-43 expressing cells as compared to wild type cells (Figure 7B, C and D), while remaining largely unaffected in the context of other mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B, C and D.

claim: Reduced actin flow was observed in TDP-43 expressing cells in comparison to WT cells and cells expressing other aggregates.
source: Reduced actin flow was also observed in TDP-43 expressing cells in comparison to WT cells and cells expressing other aggregates (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Young's modulus for cells having pathogenic aggregates of Aβ–42–2 x, FUS R521C, α-SynA30P and α-SynA53T remained similar to WT cells.
source: Young's modulus for cells having pathogenic aggregates of Aβ–42–2 x, FUS R521C, α-SynA30P and α-SynA53T remained similar to WT cells (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The stiffness was altered in case of TDP-43, similar to what was seen in HTT Q138, showing a direct correlation of cell's modulus of elasticity with actin dynamics and CME transport.
source: The stiffness was altered in case of TDP-43, similar to what was seen in HTT Q138, showing a direct correlation of cell's modulus of elasticity with actin dynamics and CME transport.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the AFM data and other observations in the manuscript.

claim: Specific pathogenic aggregates alter the physical properties of cells, by directly impacting actin dynamics and hence the CME process.
source: In our study, we demonstrate that specific pathogenic aggregates alter the physical properties of cells, by directly impacting actin dynamics and hence the CME process (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion of the study and is supported by data presented throughout the manuscript and summarized in Figure 8B.

claim: The cells with HTT Q138 and TDP-43 aggregates were observed to have increased Young's modulus compared to WT cells indicating stiffening of cells.
source: The cells with HTT Q138 and TDP-43 aggregates were observed to have increased Young's modulus compared to WT cells indicating stiffening of cells.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding based on AFM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Recovery of stiffness of the cells upon overexpression of actin binding proteins (Hip1 or Arp3) reverts cells towards the WT.
source: Recovery of stiffness of the cells upon overexpression of actin binding proteins (Hip1 or Arp3) reverts cells towards the WT, providing strong support to our hypothesis.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding based on AFM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mechanical response of cells can be used as a biomarker for actin mediated altered cell behavior in the presence of pathogenic protein aggregates.
source: More importantly, our AFM results show that mechanical response of cells can be used as a biomarker for actin mediated altered cell behavior in the presence of pathogenic protein aggregates.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the AFM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The toxicity caused by pathogenic protein aggregates may be due to a reorganization of other proteins, organelles and cellular pathways rendering them dysfunctional.
source: Further, our results demonstrate that the toxicity caused by pathogenic protein aggregates may be due to a reorganization of other proteins, organelles and cellular pathways rendering them dysfunctional (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript and summarized in Figure 8B.

claim: Rescuing some of the functions affected by pathogenic aggregates may work towards reducing neurotoxicity even in the continued presence of pathogenic aggregates.
source: Rescuing some of these functions may indeed work towards reducing neurotoxicity even in the continued presence of pathogenic aggregates.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the rescue experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The extent of observed change in CCS speed and directionality varied depending on the mutant protein present, suggesting that specific interactions may be responsible for the phenotype.
source: The extent of observed change in CCS speed and directionality varied depending on the mutant protein present, suggesting that specific interactions may be responsible for the phenotype, rather than merely the physical presence of an aggregate in the cell.
evidence: The claim is stated as an interpretation of the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The most drastic changes resulting in a complete block in CCS movement were observed in the context of HTT Q138 and TDP-43.
source: The most drastic changes resulting in a complete block in CCS movement were observed in the context of HTT Q138 and TDP-43.
evidence: The claim is stated as a summary of the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Alterations in CCS movement correlated with changes in actin dynamics as reflected by changes in filopodia length, lifetimes and actin flow.
source: Furthermore, these alterations in CCS movement also correlated with changes in actin dynamics as reflected by changes in filopodia length, lifetimes and actin flow (Figure 2 and Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is stated as a summary of the data presented in Figure 2 and Figure 7.

claim: The branching function of Arp2/3 is essential for CME.
source: Together, these indicate that the branching function of Arp2/3 is essential for CME, and that the altered function of Arp2/3 by HTT Q138 aggregates may be one of several possible mechanisms by which CME is inhibited in Huntington's disease.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The altered function of Arp2/3 by HTT Q138 aggregates may be one of several possible mechanisms by which CME is inhibited in Huntington's disease.
source: Together, these indicate that the branching function of Arp2/3 is essential for CME, and that the altered function of Arp2/3 by HTT Q138 aggregates may be one of several possible mechanisms by which CME is inhibited in Huntington's disease.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Overexpressing specific proteins that are sequestered into Huntingtin aggregates may help to reduce the toxic effects of the aggregates.
source: This is in agreement with previously published data which demonstrates that overexpression of specific proteins that are sequestered into Huntingtin aggregates may help to reduce the toxic effects of the aggregates (Hosp et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hosp et al., 2017.

claim: Overexpressing Hip1 and Arp2/3 ameliorates Huntingtin aggregate-induced loss of function and restore cellular processes.
source: Our study suggests that overexpressing Hip1 and Arp2/3 ameliorates Huntingtin aggregate-induced loss of function and restore cellular processes (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion of the study and is supported by data presented in the manuscript and summarized in Figure 8B.

claim: As the available number of Arp2/3 molecules increase, internalization depth increased in a shorter span of time.
source: Previous reports have demonstrated a tight correlation between the availability/distribution of Hip1R, Arp2/3 complex and endocytic rate and efficiency (Akamatsu et al., 2020). As the available number of Arp2/3 molecules increase, internalization depth increased in a shorter span of time.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Akamatsu et al., 2020.

claim: The distribution of Hip1R regulated the endocytosis rate and extent, presumably by regulating the recruitment and distribution of Arp2/3 complexes on the surface of the growing endocytic pit.
source: Further, while the distribution of Arp2/3 did not affect endocytic efficiency, the distribution of Hip1R regulated the endocytosis rate and extent, presumably by regulating the recruitment and distribution of Arp2/3 complexes on the surface of the growing endocytic pit.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text based on previous reports, with the mechanism being speculative.

claim: The ratio of branching to capping protein regulates stiffness of the actin network.
source: In vitro experiments have also revealed that the ratio of branching to capping protein regulates stiffness of the actin network.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text based on in vitro experiments.

claim: Network stiffness increased as either capping or branching protein concentration was increased.
source: Network stiffness increased as either capping or branching protein concentration was increased (Pujol et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pujol et al., 2012.

claim: Network stiffness is dependent on regulating a balance between branching and capping, and an alteration in these may affect stiffness and endocytic efficiency.
source: However, this points to the fact that network stiffness is dependent on regulating a balance between branching and capping, and that an alteration in these may affect stiffness and endocytic efficiency.
evidence: The claim is stated as an interpretation of the cited work.

claim: Considerable exchange exists between the membrane associated and soluble pools of clathrin light chain.
source: Previous studies looking at the FRAP of the clathrin light chain reveal that considerable exchange exists between the membrane associated and soluble pools of the protein (Wu et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wu et al., 2001 and Wu et al., 2003.

claim: Availability/exchange of clathrin at the sites of CME is compromised in the presence of HTT Q138 and TDP-43 aggregates.
source: These results indicate that availability/exchange of clathrin at the sites of CME is compromised in both these cases, in a manner hitherto unknown.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the FRAP data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The changes observed in CME in the context of HTT Q138 and TDP-43 may be dependent on the actin cytoskeleton, whereas this may not be the case in the context of other aggregates.
source: Our results suggest that the changes observed in CME in the context of HTT Q138 and TDP-43 may be dependent on the actin cytoskeleton, whereas this may not be the case in the context of other aggregates.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A loss of CME in embryonic stem cells results in an altered organization of the actin cytoskeleton and an increased cellular stiffness.
source: Previous work from our lab has demonstrated that a loss of CME in embryonic stem cells results in an altered organization of the actin cytoskeleton and an increased cellular stiffness (Mote et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mote et al., 2020.

claim: The mechanical response observed in the presence of HTT Q138 and TDP-43 aggregates appears to be linked to the altered and less dynamic state of actin organization.
source: The mechanical response by measuring the Young's modulus, observed in the presence of HTT Q138 and TDP-43 aggregates also appears to be linked to the altered and less dynamic state of actin organization.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the AFM data and actin dynamics data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The branched actin network is known to generate force required in many cellular processes including endocytosis, with alterations in this network directly limiting force transmission.
source: The branched actin network is known to generate force required in many cellular processes including endocytosis, with alterations in this network directly limiting force transmission (Goode et al., 2015; Lacy et al., 2018; Planade et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Goode et al., 2015; Lacy et al., 2018; Planade et al., 2019.

claim: A 'Goldilocks' state of the branched actin network is required for sufficient and efficient force generation during CME, where it is neither too soft, nor too stiff, but in an intermediate, dynamic state.
source: This suggests that a 'Goldilocks' state of the branched actin network is required for sufficient and efficient force generation during CME, where it is neither too soft, nor too stiff, but in an intermediate, dynamic state.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The rescue of neurodegeneration driven by pathogenic Huntingtin by the overexpression of actin binding proteins indicates that the remodelling of the actin cytoskeleton contributes largely to the aggregate-driven neurotoxicity.
source: The rescue of neurodegeneration driven by pathogenic Huntingtin by the overexpression of actin binding proteins, indicates that the remodelling of the actin cytoskeleton contributes largely to the aggregate-driven neurotoxicity.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the rescue experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The similarity in phenotypes observed in the context of CCS movement across different cell types from multiple organisms throws up interesting possibilities for screening potential molecular candidates in the context of Huntington's disease.
source: Further, the similarity in phenotypes observed in the context of CCS movement across different cell types from multiple organisms throws up interesting possibilities for screening potential molecular candidates in the context of Huntington's disease.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Overexpression of the monomeric versus the dimeric form of α-synuclein in the lamprey giant reticulospinal synapses demonstrated a block of CME at different stages indicative of their ability to interfere at different stages of CME.
source: Overexpression of the monomeric versus the dimeric form of α-synuclein in the lamprey giant reticulospinal synapses demonstrated a block of CME at different stages indicative of their ability to interfere at different stages of CME, suggestive of a differential interaction with proteins (Medeiros et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Medeiros et al., 2017.

claim: TDP-43 knockdown has been shown to alter the number and motility of Rab11-positive recycling endosomes.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schwenk et al., 2016.

claim: The loss of HTT has been shown to result in the altered activation status of cofilin, thereby resulting in altered actin dynamics.
source: TDP-43 knockdown has also been shown to alter the number and motility of Rab11-positive recycling endosomes (Schwenk et al., 2016), while the loss of HTT has been shown to result in the altered activation status of cofilin, thereby resulting in altered actin dynamics (Wennagel et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wennagel et al., 2022.

claim: The toxicity associated with TDP-43 was enhanced upon inhibiting endocytosis.
source: Further, the toxicity associated with TDP-43 was enhanced upon inhibiting endocytosis (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2017.

claim: Nwk/FCHSD2, Dap160/Intersectin and WASP play a role in regulating actin assembly at synapses.
source: Recent work has highlighted a role for Nwk/FCHSD2, Dap160/Intersectin and WASP in regulating actin assembly at synapses (Del Signore et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Del Signore et al., 2021.

claim: Intersectin has been shown to associate with mutant forms of HTT and enhance its aggregation resulting in increased neuro-toxicity.
source: Interestingly, Intersectin has been shown to associate with mutant forms of HTT and enhance its aggregation resulting in increased neuro-toxicity (Scappini et al., 2007).
